## 

During the summer semester of my Master's program, I worked on a remote internship with Northwestern University under Dr. Wenna Xi, where I investigated the relationship between substance use and four suicide-related outcomes among U.S. high school students using nationally representative Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) data from 2017–2023.

I analyzed 11 substance-use variables, including cigarette smoking, vaping, alcohol, marijuana, prescription pain medication misuse, and other drug use. I examined four outcomes: seriously considering suicide, making a suicide plan, attempting suicide, and being injured in a suicide attempt. I used four logistic regression models to evaluate these associations while accounting for age, sex, and race.

Across the four outcomes, prescription pain medication misuse and inhalant use showed consistent associations with higher odds of suicide-related outcomes. For serious injury during a suicide attempt, prescription pain medication misuse was associated with 3.08 times the odds of the outcome, while heroin use was associated with 2.86 times the odds. Marijuana and alcohol use were also associated with higher odds of serious injury. These findings highlight the importance of looking at different types of substance use when studying suicide risk in teens, and allows us to identify where mental health support is needed.
